As somoene who WENT to a trade school, be very, VERY picky. The vast majority of trade schools are simply pumping people through without teaching Anything. I know, first hand, this is true of the mechanics and technology fields (the 2 in which I've personal experience over the last 3 decades), but have heard the same from a huge swath of people who've been through "trade schools".

Better option would be a community college that has a vocational department. You'll get not only Real training in a trade, but a college degree to boot. It may not seem important, but you'll have a leg up on everyone else in that given trade and have first right of refusal when it comes to promotions strictly due to that degree.

Beyond that, I fully agree that option for a career path, it's hard to beat a trade like plumber and electrician. They will be in demand till the end of time. Solar/turbines seems to be a hot and growing market right now. I know one guy who's in wind turbines and is being run ragged because there simply aren't enough people to do the work (and they pay him insane sums of money he has no time to spend, dude will be able to retire at 40 if it keeps going this way and he can keep it up).

Trade schools are all about what you put into them. Yes, they exist solely as a for profit business, but that doesn't mean you can't get something out of the program you're in. Those who don't do the work can probably barely skate by, however those who do put in the work are miles ahead of everyone else.

How much work you put in doesn't matter if all they teach is "Read the fucking manual", and that is ALL they teach in mechanics trade schools. Nothing else. I was top of my class, not saying much when there were probably 6~8 people who weren't there because it was a requirement for parole (yes, most technical trade schools are filled with criminals who have to meet education requirements for parole) and I doubt the average reading ability exceeded 6th grade.

Anyone interested in auto/motorcycle mechanics would be better suited in buying a clunker, the factory service manual and rebuilding said clunker from the ground up. It'll be cheaper, you'll learn more AND have something to show for it at the end.
